title: Loving without clinging
hook: the fourth: equanimity, loving without clinging

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was mudita: gladness at someone else's good fortune. Your line was more joy in the world. Today, the last of the four boundless states.

A parent stands at the curb outside a dorm. The car is empty now. The boxes are upstairs, the bed is made, the hug has happened twice. Every instinct says: stay, check once more, call tonight, call tomorrow morning too. And the kid, halfway up the steps, turns and waves, ready to go. Loving someone and letting them walk up those steps can feel like opposites. One Buddhist word holds them together, and in English it goes by a word that can sound cold: equanimity.
screen: `A PARENT AT THE CURB.` → `STAY, OR LET THEM GO?` → `THE FOURTH BOUNDLESS STATE.`

segments.voice: Upekkha means looking on with an even heart. It isn't a fifth feeling added to the other three. It's the balance that keeps loving-kindness, compassion and gladness from tipping over into grabbing, drowning or needing. It has a counterfeit too. Buddhaghosa, in his Path of Purification, names its near enemy: a blank, unknowing not-caring that only looks calm. A shrug is not upekkha. The parent who stops caring has missed it as surely as the one who can't drive away. Its far enemies are greed and resentment: grabbing at people, and pushing them away. Equanimity sits between them, close enough to love, loose enough not to hold on. The reflection Buddhaghosa gives for it rests on a teaching from the suttas: beings are the owners of their own deeds. That sounds stern, but turned toward someone you love, it's a release. Their life is theirs. Their choices are theirs. You can wish them every good thing, and help where help is wanted, without carrying the weight of steering it all. In these texts, upekkha doesn't end the love of the first three states. It's what lets that love last.
screen: `AN EVEN HEART.` · `NOT A SHRUG.` · `NOT GRABBING, NOT PUSHING AWAY.` · `THEIR LIFE IS THEIR OWN.` · then, large: `UPEKKHA.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one person you love and worry about, hold them warmly for a few breaths, and notice where the love has a grip in it: wanting them to choose a certain way, needing to know they're all right. Breathing out, loosen that grip a little without letting go of the warmth, and if it helps, let a quiet thought sit there: your life is your own, and I wish you well. If you pray, you can place them in a prayer from your own tradition.
Upekkha. Equanimity: an even heart that keeps on loving without clinging, the fourth of the four boundless states. Today's word.
Your line: even-hearted. Not a shrug, and not a grip, but a love that lasts. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: In Buddhaghosa's manual, equanimity (upekkha) is developed after the other three boundless states, by reflecting that beings are the owners of their own deeds so that love stays warm without turning into clinging.

chat.meaning: Buddhaghosa calls blank not-caring equanimity's near enemy. Upekkha is an even heart: close enough to love, loose enough not to hold on.
